raw_response:
I’m 76 now, so I won’t chase every last jin of yield. On 8 mu, the main thing is to keep the household income steady and not stretch our cash or labor too far. I’ll keep 5 mu in the usual wheat-maize rotation because that is still the safest system here in Quzhou, and I’ll keep 3 mu in cotton since I know that crop well, but I won’t expand it because cotton needs too much hand work at picking. I have high education and long experience, so I do look at rates and timing more carefully than before, but in the end I still farm by what has worked on my own land: enough fertilizer to avoid visible hunger, irrigation at the key stages, and not too much risk on new inputs. With only 2 people in the household and some off-farm work, I will depend on simple field operations, a bit of hired help, and conservative management rather than pushing for maximum output.

For wheat, I’ll use the better part of the land and plant on time in October with an improved local variety. I’ll put most phosphorus and potassium in as base fertilizer, split nitrogen between sowing and spring topdressing, and irrigate at the important stages because our well water costs money but missing water in wheat usually costs more in yield. After wheat harvest, I’ll move quickly into summer maize on the same 5 mu with direct seeding and light tillage so I don’t lose the planting window. For cotton, I’ll keep the area limited, use moderate fertilizer, and watch insects closely because cotton can eat up money fast if I start spraying too often. Overall, I’d rather spend a bit more on the wheat-maize land, which is more stable, and keep cotton at a manageable scale.
